e.etymology: A French pet form of Marguerite (Margaret), from Greek margarites (pearl). It has long stood as a name in its own right.

assoc.t: Margot Robbie, star of Barbie

e.etymology: From Old Norse Freyja (lady, mistress), the Norse goddess of love, beauty and war. The spelling Freya began as a Scottish form and is a favorite in Britain.

assoc.t: Freya, Norse goddess of love, beauty and war

e.etymology: From Irish Fionn (fair, white), the name of the legendary hero Fionn mac Cumhaill. A separate Old Norse name Finnr meant a Sami or Finnish person.

assoc.t: Huckleberry Finn, Mark Twain's runaway hero
Finn, the ex-stormtrooper in the Star Wars sequels
Finn the Human of Adventure Time
a Finn, a person from Finland

e.etymology: From an English occupational surname, common in the southwest of England, for a fuller: a worker who cleaned and thickened woven cloth.

assoc.t: Tucker Carlson, conservative TV commentator

e.note: Rhymes with a common vulgar insult, an easy route to teasing.

e.etymology: From the English word messiah, from Hebrew mashiach (anointed), the title of the promised deliverer and, for Christians, of Jesus. Its use as a given name is recent and American.

assoc.t: religious title for the promised savior; Jesus to Christians
Handel's Messiah, oratorio with the Hallelujah chorus

e.note: A religious title that some find presumptuous; in 2013 a Tennessee judge tried to order a baby Messiah renamed.

e.etymology: From the English word for a small glowing piece of coal or wood left in a fire. A modern word name that also echoes Amber and Emma.

assoc.t: Ember Lumen, fiery heroine of Pixar's Elemental
Ember temperature-controlled smart mugs

e.etymology: A Scottish name from Calum, the Gaelic form of Latin Columba (dove), honoring Saint Columba, who founded the monastery of Iona. Also a shortening of the surname McCallum.

e.meaning: jet, the black gemstone; also the aircraft
e.etymology: From the English word jet, the glossy black gemstone and later the aircraft, and from the surname Jett. Rock singer Joan Jett made it familiar.

assoc.t: Joan Jett, rock singer of I Love Rock 'n Roll
sounds like jet, the aircraft
Jett, a playable agent in the video game Valorant

e.etymology: A modern American spelling modeled on Hawaiian names that end in lani (sky, heaven), such as Keilani and Kailani. It spread in the United States with R&B singer Kehlani.

assoc.t: Kehlani, R&B singer who goes by the one name

e.etymology: From Irish Caoimhín, Old Irish Cóemgen (dear or handsome birth), the name of the Irish saint who founded Glendalough. It spread beyond Ireland in the mid-1900s.

assoc.t: Kevin McCallister, the boy left behind in Home Alone
internet joke name for a clueless guy

e.etymology: A short form of Alexander or Alexandra, from Greek Alexandros (defender of men), long used as a name in its own right for boys and girls.
From Latin Justinus, a derivative of Justus (just), borne by early saints including the second-century writer Justin Martyr. Popular in English since the 1970s.

assoc.t: pop stars Justin Bieber and Justin Timberlake
Justin Boots, Western boot maker
Justin's nut butters and peanut butter cups

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el (who is like God?), the name of the archangel.
namesakes: Miguel de Cervantes (author of Don Quixote)

assoc.t: Miguel, the boy hero of Pixar's Coco
Miguel, R&B singer who goes by the one name

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Alexander, from Greek Alexandros: alexein (to defend) plus aner, andros (man).

assoc.t: Alejandro, 2010 Lady Gaga hit song

e.etymology: From an English surname, a variant of Stitson, from Stidston in Devon: the Old English personal name Stithweard plus tun (farmstead). Hat maker John B. Stetson made it famous.

assoc.t: Stetson cowboy hats
Stetson cologne
Stetson University in Florida

e.etymology: A respelling of Carter, an English occupational surname for someone who hauled goods by cart.

assoc.t: President Jimmy Carter, by sound
Carter's children's clothing, by sound

e.etymology: The feminine form of the Roman family name Valerius, from Latin valere (to be healthy, to be strong). Valerie is the French form of the same name.
From Hebrew Shiloh, the town in the Bible where the Ark of the Covenant was kept, and a word in Genesis 49 that some read as a title of the Messiah. Its meaning is debated.
namesakes: Shiloh Jolie-Pitt (child of Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt)

assoc.t: Battle of Shiloh, 1862 Civil War battle in Tennessee
Shiloh, biblical town that housed the Ark
Shiloh, the beagle of the children's novel and film

e.etymology: From a Scottish clan surname, Gaelic MacCoinnich, son of Coinneach (Kenneth, handsome). The z comes from misreading the old Scots letter yogh. A girls' name in North America since the 1970s.
namesakes: Mackenzie Phillips (actress, One Day at a Time)

assoc.t: Mackenzie River, Canada's longest river

e.meaning: the month of June, named for the goddess Juno
e.etymology: From the month, Latin Junius, named for the Roman goddess Juno. Given to girls born in June since the late 1800s, and a top name of the 1920s.
namesakes: June Cleaver (the mother in Leave It to Beaver)
June Osborne (heroine of The Handmaid's Tale)

assoc.t: June, the sixth month of the year

e.etymology: The feminine of Ximeno or Jimeno, a medieval Spanish and Basque name linked to Basque seme (son). Jimena Díaz, wife of El Cid, is its best-known early bearer.
e.note: English speakers often stumble over the X; it is said like an H.

e.etymology: An American coinage of the 2000s made to rhyme with Jayden, Brayden and Aidan, with the fashionable initial Z.
From a surname: either a Scottish place name of Pictish origin meaning meadow dwelling, or English for a dweller at the house in the dale. The Texas city honors Vice President George M. Dallas.
namesakes: Dallas Winston (tough greaser in The Outsiders)

assoc.t: Dallas, Texas, home of the Cowboys
Dallas, 1980s TV drama about the Ewing oil family

e.etymology: From Arabic amira (princess, commander), the feminine of Amir. It is also used in Hebrew, where it is read as treetop.

e.meaning: woman of the family, by one reading
e.etymology: From French Geneviève, Latin Genovefa, the fifth-century patron saint of Paris. The roots are either Germanic words for kin and woman or a Celtic word for family.
From Greek Petros (stone, rock), a translation of the Aramaic name Kefa that Jesus gave the apostle Simon.

assoc.t: Peter Pan, the boy who never grows up
Saint Peter, apostle and first pope
Peter Parker, Spider-Man's alter ego
Peter Rabbit, Beatrix Potter's mischievous rabbit
peter, dated slang for penis

e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Riagáin, descendant of Riagán, a personal name of uncertain meaning. Its use as a first name is American and followed Ronald Reagan's presidency.

assoc.t: Ronald Reagan, fortieth US president

e.note: So tied to President Ronald Reagan that some people will read it as a political statement.

e.etymology: The medieval Spanish form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva (my God is an oath). It reached England in the 1200s and was borne by queens of Spain, Portugal and England.
From a Scottish surname taken from Gaelic cnoc (round hill). Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt's choice of it for a son in 2008 put it on the map.
namesakes: John Knox (leader of the Scottish Reformation)

assoc.t: Fort Knox, the US gold depository in Kentucky
Amanda Knox, American acquitted of murder in Italy
Knox unflavored gelatin

e.etymology: A recent American coinage that joins oak, the tree, to the popular -lynn ending, on the pattern of Oakley and Brooklyn.
From the English surname and place name Blakeley, Old English blaec (black, dark) plus leah (woodland clearing). Its use as a girls' name is recent and American.
The Spanish form of Andrew, from Greek Andreas, from aner, andros (man). Andrew was the first apostle called by Jesus.
